df <- data.frame(a = 1:6, b = rep(letters[1:3],2))

x <- 'b'

This works:
group_by(df,b)

But why doesn't the following work?

group_by(df, x)

More crucially, neither does this:

group_by(df, as.symbol(x)) #failing with "(list) object cannot be coerced to type 'symbol'"

And, of course, is there a fix?

messages.subject: When to use plyr's rename function instead of dplyr's
messages.subject_clean: When to use plyr's rename function instead of dplyr's
messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

I just tried out the new rename() function in dplyr, which works like select() but keeps even the variables you didn't ask for or rename. It's a nice addition to dplyr and it fits in well with how dplyr works. However, it may not always be the best way to rename variables. The plyr package also has a rename() function, and it uses R's built-in names() function. So if you had a large data set and all you wanted to do was rename some variables (perhaps to match names before stacking the data set with another via rbind() or rbind_list()), it would be much more efficient to use plyr's rename() as the dplyr version would process the whole data frame rather than simply changing the names as they're stored in the relatively tiny names attribute.

Cheers,
Bob

Here is a quick benchmark. Both are fast, plyr is faster.

library(plyr)
library(hflights)

system.time(
    sapply(
        1:10000,
        function(x) {
            foo <- rename(hflights,
                          c(Year="year",
                          Month="month",
                          DayofMonth="dayofmonth",
                          DayOfWeek="dayofweek"))
            return(NULL)
        }))

  ##  user  system elapsed
  ## 2.140   0.180   2.364

detach(package:plyr, unload=TRUE)
library(dplyr)

system.time(
    sapply(
        1:10000,
        function(x) {
            foo <- rename(hflights,
                          year=Year,
                          month=Month,
                          dayofmonth=DayofMonth,
                          dayofweek=DayOfWeek)
            return(NULL)

messages.subject: Use of ORDER_BY in subqueries
messages.body_plain:
Use of ORDER_BY in subqueries is troublesome for SQL Server. It cannot be present in subqueries except in very limiting circumstances <http://stackoverflow.com/questions/985921/sql-error-with-order-by-in-subquery>. This means some things break. For e.g.

```
pd <- tbl(dbsrc, from="table")
# Has field name days
pd %>% arrange(days)

Unable to retrieve JDBC result set for SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT "x", "days", "y", "x"
FROM "table"
ORDER BY "days") AS "master" (The ORDER BY clause is invalid in views, inline functions, derived tables, and subqueries, unless TOP is also specified.)
```

I suspect the error here is that in printing details of result, it needs to evaluate number of rows, but can't because of the limitation on ORDER BY in SQL SERVER.

What's the best strategy to resolve this? Is there some way that I can get arrange to evaluate the subquery remotely and then provide the result to outside SELECT query? Or do I need to evaluate the internal query locally and then count rows with the base NROW() function? The latter seems pretty counterproductive.

#' @export

messages.subject: Re: t.test and summarising multiple columns
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

Here are a couple of approaches using both plyr and tidyr.

(1) Write a function that returns a data frame of the means, SDs and
p-value for the t-test of each numeric variable by vs and then call it
with do().

library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)

# Base data frame with which to work. It is a molten data frame
# with the categorical/count variables cyl, am, gear and carb removed
# gather() is akin to reshape2::melt()

DFm <- mtcars %>% select(mpg, disp:vs) %>% gather("var", "val", -vs)

## Function to apply to each data split
f <- function(DF)
{
   pv <- t.test(val ~ vs, data = DF)[["p.value"]]
   means <- tapply(DF$val, DF$vs, mean)
   sds <- tapply(DF$val, DF$vs, sd)
   stats <- c(means, sds, pv)
   names(stats) <- c("mean0", "mean1", "sd0", "sd1", "p.value")
   data.frame(as.list(stats))
}

# Apply it through the pipeline
DFm %>% group_by(var) %>% do(f(.))

## (2) Pure dplyr/tidyr approach

# Start by computing the data frame of summary stats
# by variable (rows) and vs (cols) - akin to reshape2::dcast()
DFstats <- DFm %>%
             group_by(var, vs) %>%
             summarise_each(funs(mean, sd), val) %>%
             gather(stat, statval, mean, sd) %>%
             unite(stat_vs, stat, vs) %>%
             spread(stat_vs, statval)

# Tack on the p-values from the t-tests
cbind(DFstats, DFm %>%
                group_by(var) %>%
                do(data.frame(pval = t.test(val ~ vs, data = .)[["p.value"]])))

Dennis

> Thanks for the write-up Hadley.
>
> Is it a requirement that there be a DBI compliant interface to the database in question? Is it unlikely that dplyr could use RODBC in the future?
>
> With regard to MS SQL Server, I don't think we've had a DBI-compliant interface until quite recently (see: https://github.com/agstudy/rsqlserver) and it looks like it's still relatively early in development.
>
> I'm having some trouble getting it up and running unfortunately (will contact the package author for help).
>
>
> On Thursday, January 30, 2014 6:33:08 AM UTC+8, Hadley Wickham wrote:
> > > In the R studio blog, you mention "adding a new backend is a matter of
> > > implementing a handful of S3 methods." Could you expand on this? I'm sure
> > > its documented somewhere, I'm just having trouble finding it. Might it just
> > > be something like this?
> > > https://github.com/hadley/dplyr/blob/master/R/src-postgres.r but for our db
> > > of choice?
> >
> > Right, it's not documented anywhere, but it's not too hard. Here's a
> > quick stab at how I'd go about implementing a new backend.
> >
> > # src
> >
> > * Start with creating a new src to represent the backend. Assuming
> > we're going to create a src for mssql, you'd call it src_mssql, and
> > you'd follow the pattern of an existing src, eg. src-mysql.r.
> > Basically, all the object needs to store is information about how to
> > connect to the database, and it should implement a method of
> > brief_desc() to briefly describe the source.
> >
> > * Next implement the database level methods in dbi-s3.r:
> > dbi_connect(), db_list_tables(), db_has_table(), db_data_type(). These
> > should be fairly obvious once you look at the existing
> > implementations.
> >
> > * With these implemented you should be able to connect to a src and
> > get a useful description, including a list of tables. Iterate until
> > that works.
> >
> > # tbl
> >
> > * Next implement the tbl method for your data source. This will probably just be
> >
> > tbl.src_mssql <- function(src, from, ...) {
> >   tbl_sql("mssql", src = src, from = from, ...)
> > }
> >
> > * Then implement the query related methods in dbi-s3.r: qry_fields(),
> > table_fields(), qry_fetch(), qry_explain(). Again, these aren't
> > documented, but are pretty simple and there are lots of existing code.
> >
> > * Once you've done this you should be able to connect to a tbl in your
> > new source, and get a reasonable print out. Iterate until that works.
> >
> > * If the database is not ANSI SQL compliant, you'll need to provide
> > methods for the sql_* methods in dbi-s3.r: sql_begin_trans(),
> > sql_commit(), sql_insert_into(), sql_create_indexes(), sql_analyze().
> >
> > * At this point, summarise(), filter(), arrange(), mutate() etc should all work
> >
> > # sql translation
> >
> > * To finish off, you can add custom R -> SQL translation by providing
> > a method for translate_env. This function should return an object
> > created by sql_variant(). See existing methods for examples.
> >
> > If you're familiar with how your database works, and at least one
> > other database that dplyr already supports, this should be reasonably
> > simple, and I'm happy to help if you get stuck.  It's also possible
> > that a new database backend may need new methods - I'm also happy to
> > add those as needed.
> >
> > Hadley
> >
> > --
> > http://had.co.nz/

messages.body_plain:
Dear ManipulatRs,

I'm trying to convert most of my processes over to dplyr away from plyr and merge(), but I've run into a situation when chaining joins.

When the join column name is the same between joins it seems to work fine, but when you mix it up it does not work.

MRE below.

Any ideas? Is this a bug?

Brandon

asdf2 <- data.frame(PLTID = LETTERS[26:1], length = runif(26))
asdf3 <- data.frame(PLTID = LETTERS[26:1], arc = runif(26))

inner_join(asdf1, asdf2, by="PLTID") %>%
inner_join(., asdf3, by="PLTID")

jkl1 <- data.frame(PLTID = LETTERS[1:26], width = runif(26))

inner_join(., jkl3, by=c("PLTID", "CODE"))

To install:

devtools::install_github("imanuelcostigan/RSQLServer@feature/dplyr")

Thanks!

I've been working on getting dplyr interfaces set up <https://github.com/imanuelcostigan/RSQLServer/issues/4> but it looks like its going to be hard work. I'd be happy to coordinate work in this respect - although I think I might need to reach out to Hadley once I've had time to get my head around the dplyr framework a bit more comprehensively.
>
>
> On Thursday, 30 January 2014 10:18:44 UTC+11, TMOD wrote:
> > Thanks for the write-up Hadley.
> >
> > Is it a requirement that there be a DBI compliant interface to the database in question? Is it unlikely that dplyr could use RODBC in the future?
> >
> > With regard to MS SQL Server, I don't think we've had a DBI-compliant interface until quite recently (see: https://github.com/agstudy/rsqlserver) and it looks like it's still relatively early in development.
> >
> > I'm having some trouble getting it up and running unfortunately (will contact the package author for help).
> >
> >
> > On Thursday, January 30, 2014 6:33:08 AM UTC+8, Hadley Wickham wrote:
> > > > In the R studio blog, you mention "adding a new backend is a matter of
> > > > implementing a handful of S3 methods." Could you expand on this? I'm sure
> > > > its documented somewhere, I'm just having trouble finding it. Might it just
> > > > be something like this?
> > > > https://github.com/hadley/dplyr/blob/master/R/src-postgres.r but for our db
> > > > of choice?
> > >
> > > Right, it's not documented anywhere, but it's not too hard. Here's a
> > > quick stab at how I'd go about implementing a new backend.
> > >
> > > # src
> > >
> > > * Start with creating a new src to represent the backend. Assuming
> > > we're going to create a src for mssql, you'd call it src_mssql, and
> > > you'd follow the pattern of an existing src, eg. src-mysql.r.
> > > Basically, all the object needs to store is information about how to
> > > connect to the database, and it should implement a method of
> > > brief_desc() to briefly describe the source.
> > >
> > > * Next implement the database level methods in dbi-s3.r:
> > > dbi_connect(), db_list_tables(), db_has_table(), db_data_type(). These
> > > should be fairly obvious once you look at the existing
> > > implementations.
> > >
> > > * With these implemented you should be able to connect to a src and
> > > get a useful description, including a list of tables. Iterate until
> > > that works.
> > >
> > > # tbl
> > >
> > > * Next implement the tbl method for your data source. This will probably just be
> > >
> > > tbl.src_mssql <- function(src, from, ...) {
> > >   tbl_sql("mssql", src = src, from = from, ...)
> > > }
> > >
> > > * Then implement the query related methods in dbi-s3.r: qry_fields(),
> > > table_fields(), qry_fetch(), qry_explain(). Again, these aren't
> > > documented, but are pretty simple and there are lots of existing code.
> > >
> > > * Once you've done this you should be able to connect to a tbl in your
> > > new source, and get a reasonable print out. Iterate until that works.
> > >
> > > * If the database is not ANSI SQL compliant, you'll need to provide
> > > methods for the sql_* methods in dbi-s3.r: sql_begin_trans(),
> > > sql_commit(), sql_insert_into(), sql_create_indexes(), sql_analyze().
> > >
> > > * At this point, summarise(), filter(), arrange(), mutate() etc should all work
> > >
> > > # sql translation
> > >
> > > * To finish off, you can add custom R -> SQL translation by providing
> > > a method for translate_env. This function should return an object
> > > created by sql_variant(). See existing methods for examples.
> > >
> > > If you're familiar with how your database works, and at least one
> > > other database that dplyr already supports, this should be reasonably
> > > simple, and I'm happy to help if you get stuck.  It's also possible
> > > that a new database backend may need new methods - I'm also happy to
> > > add those as needed.
> > >
> > > Hadley
> > >
> > > --
> > > http://had.co.nz/

messages.subject: slice() vs. head() (and do)
messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

I just had a "Doh!" moment I thought I'd share. I had not really caught on to the importance of the slice() function. It seemed just like head() or tail(). Then I used head() on a data frame that had been run through group_by(). It only printed the head of the whole data frame since it has no idea that the grouped indices were set.  slice() did it by group of course. That's where do() comes in. It can make any function work on group_by info and so it can make head() work like slice() on grouped data, but slice() is so much easier.

Cheers,
Bob
